 shares no code
 8 checks: pass / fail
Everything inside the grey box is one process. The operation applier and the undo engine both call the tag propagator. The checker also reads seed.jsonl and ops.jsonl so it can work out the expected result on its own.
### The parts and what each one does
Python 3.11+
The language. Its standard library already includes SQLite (sqlite3), JSON, UUIDs and a command-line parser, so nothing has to be installed.
graph.db
One SQLite file. It holds the live graph and the journal. SQLite features used: transactions, foreign keys, unique indexes, and recursive queries.
load
Loader. Starts a new database file, replacing an old one. Reads seed.jsonl and fills the nodes and edges tables, then computes tags once for the whole graph.
apply
Operation applier. Runs ops.jsonl in order. Five kinds of operation: edit a node, add an edge, re-point an edge, ingest a node by name, delete a subtree. Each is described under "What can change the graph" below. When ingest creates a node, its id is built from the op_id and the name, so the same files give the same ids on every run. A delete moves what it removes into the journal. A contains arrow that would make a node its own ancestor is refused: the operation is stored as rejected and changes nothing, so a loop never gets into the graph. The same happens to an operation that names a node or arrow that is not live. An op_id names one operation: when it is already in the database, the line is skipped if it is that same operation, so applying a file again is harmless, and apply stops with an error before changing anything if it is a different one.
undo <op_id>
Undo engine. Walks the journal rows of one delete, decides restored, merged or skipped for each, writes the result, prints the report. It only accepts the op_id of a subtree delete. For any other operation, or an id that does not exist, it prints an error and writes nothing.
dump
Dumper. Prints every live node and edge as JSONL in one fixed order: node lines sorted by id, then edge lines sorted by from, to and type. Keys are always in the same order, inherited tags are sorted alphabetically, and own tags stay in the order they were written. Two equal graphs always print the same bytes. A node line holds id, qualified_name, type, description, owner, tags and effective_tags. An edge line holds from_id, to_id and type.
Tag propagator
One function: recompute inherited tags for a node and everything below it. Called by apply and by undo.
Store
A thin layer over sqlite3. Opens the file, turns foreign keys on, wraps each step in a transaction, and counts write statements so CRASH_AFTER=<n> can stop the process on the n-th one.
gen_fixture.py
Makes seed.jsonl and ops.jsonl from a seed number, and planted.json, which lists the nodes each planted case uses. Same seed, same files: every id and every choice comes from one random generator started with the seed. It checks its own output against the minimums the task sets and stops with an error if one is missed.
checker.py
A separate program that imports nothing from the tool. It replays the seed and the operations in plain Python dictionaries, then compares that with the dumps and the report for the eight checks.
### What can change the graph
These are all the kinds of change the tool knows. Every one carries who made it: a person or the ingest.
Edit a node
By a person. Sets the description, the owner or the tags of one live node. A tag change is passed down to everything the node contains. An edit from ingest is refused, because ingest never sets description, owner or tags.
Add an arrow
By a person or by ingest. Adds a contains or references arrow between two live nodes.
Re-point an arrow
By a person or by ingest. Moves one end of an existing arrow to another node. It counts as two changes: the old arrow is taken away and the new one is added. Re-pointing a contains arrow moves a node under another parent.
Ingest a node by name
By ingest. If a live node already has the name, ingest updates its type. If none has it, ingest creates a node with a new id and puts it under its parent, if that parent is live. Ingest never sets description, owner or tags. An ingest from a person is refused: people do not create nodes in this tool, and only ingest sets the type.
Delete a subtree
By a person or by ingest. Removes a node, everything it contains, and every arrow that touches any of them. The inherited tags of the nodes that remain are then recomputed.
Undo a delete
By a person, with the undo command. It takes the op_id of one subtree delete. The undo is recorded as an operation of its own, so a redo can be added later.
Not part of the tool: a person creating a node, renaming a node, removing a single arrow without re-pointing it, undoing anything other than a subtree delete, redo (designed in section 4, not built yet), the 24-hour limit, and checking who is allowed to do what.
## 2The graph inside SQLite
SQLite stores tables, not graphs. A graph is two lists: a list of things and a list of arrows between them. So there are two tables. Each row in nodes is one box. Each row in edges is one arrow, written as "from this id, to that id, of this kind".
The running example is a small data catalog. Ids are shortened to n1, n2 and so on; the real ones are UUIDs.
 salesn1
 sales.ordersn2
 sales.orders.emailn3
 reports.dailyn6
 contains
 contains
 references
 nodes: one row per box
 | id | qualified_name | type | owner | tags | effective_tags
 | n1 | sales | schema | | ["finance"] | ["finance"]
 | n2 | sales.orders | table | asha | ["pii"] | ["finance","pii"]
 | n3 | sales.orders.email | column | dana | ["contact"] | ["contact","finance","pii"]
 | n6 | reports.daily | dashboard | | [] | []
 edges: one row per arrow
 | from_id | to_id | type
 | n1 | n2 | contains
 | n2 | n3 | contains
 | n6 | n2 | references
The drawing and the rows are the same information. The description column is left out of the table to keep it narrow.
### Tags that flow down from a parent
The task calls them tags. A tag set on a parent is carried by every node below it. A node has two tag columns. tags is what someone set on that node. effective_tags is worked out: the node's own tags plus the effective tags of its parent. In the table above, sales.orders.email has one tag of its own and gets pii and finance from the two nodes above it. Only contains arrows carry tags. references arrows do not.
### Walking the graph
"Everything under sales.orders" is found by a recursive query. Start with the root. Add every node it contains. Add every node those contain. Stop when a round adds nothing.
WITH RECURSIVE sub(id) AS (
 SELECT :root_id
 UNION
 SELECT e.to_id
 FROM edges e JOIN sub ON e.from_id = sub.id
 WHERE e.type = 'contains'
)
SELECT id FROM sub;
The query uses UNION, which drops a node it has already found, so the walk always ends. This matters if a contains loop ever exists, for example A contains B and B contains A. With UNION ALL, or with a depth counter inside the query, the walk goes round the loop for ever. The parents-first order that undo needs is worked out afterwards, by following the removed contains arrows down from the root.
The same walk, run downward from a node, is how the tag propagator refreshes effective_tags for a subtree: each node takes its own tags plus the already-refreshed tags of its parent.
### The tables
CREATE TABLE nodes (
 id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
 qualified_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, -- this table holds live nodes only
 type TEXT NOT NULL,
 description TEXT,
 owner TEXT,
 tags TEXT NOT NULL, -- JSON list, set by people
 effective_tags TEXT NOT NULL -- JSON list, worked out
);
CREATE TABLE edges (
 from_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES nodes(id),
 to_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES nodes(id),
 type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('contains','references')),
 PRIMARY KEY (from_id, to_id, type)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_parent ON edges(to_id) WHERE type = 'contains';
Three rules are enforced by the database itself, so no code path can break them:
- Two live nodes cannot share a name (UNIQUE on qualified_name).
- An arrow cannot point at a node that is not there (REFERENCES nodes(id), with foreign keys switched on).
- A node has at most one contains parent (the one_parent index). The graph of contains arrows is a tree. The task itself speaks of a subtree, a root and a node's parent. An operation that would give a node a second parent is stored as rejected.
### The journal
A deleted row is not thrown away. The delete moves it from the live tables into the journal tables, labelled with the delete's op_id. Undo later moves rows back one at a time and writes what it did next to each row.
ops
Every operation, with a running number, its op_id, its kind, the time it ran, whether a human or the ingest did it, and whether it was applied or rejected (with the reason). The running number is what "after the delete" means. Each undo is recorded here too, the first time it runs, as an operation of its own by a person (undo:<op_id>), so a later operation, or a redo, can tell what came after it.
removed_nodes
A copy of each node a delete removed: id, name, type, description, owner, tags, the id of its parent, and its place in parents-first order. For each of the three fields, and for the type, it also keeps who wrote it last and in which operation. Plus the columns undo fills in: outcome, reason, merged_into, waiting_on, the details the report prints for a merge, the undo that decided the row (decided_by), and for a merge what the live node held before undo changed it (prior), so a redo can put it back.
removed_edges
A copy of each arrow a delete removed, with its place in the order undo takes them. Plus outcome, reason, waiting_on, where the arrow points now if it was moved, and the undo that decided it.
field_writes
For each node and each of description, owner, tags and type: who wrote it last, and in which operation. This lets undo tell "empty because nobody wrote it" from "a person cleared it on purpose", and lets the type follow the same "most recent wins" rule.
edge_removals
Every arrow a person re-pointed away from its old target, with the number of the operation. Undo uses it so that it never puts back an arrow a person took away after the delete.
effective_tags is never copied into the journal. It is always worked out again from what is live at that moment.

### What undo does, in order
- Take the removed nodes of that delete from the journal, parents before children.
- For each node, decide one of three outcomes (next figure), make the change, put the arrow from its parent back, and refresh the tags of that node and everything below it. All of that is one transaction.
- Then take the remaining removed arrows (the references ones) and decide each one the same way.
- Then retry any rows of earlier undos that were waiting on this delete.
- Print the report from the journal rows.

The name is checked first. A node whose name is taken is always merged, wherever its parent is. A node that sat at the top level before the delete has no parent to check and is restored.
### Name clashes: two ids, one name
Every node has two identities. The id is for the machine and is never reused. The name is for people and only has to be unique among live nodes. A delete frees the name. The ingest then creates a node with that name and a fresh id. At undo time two nodes claim sales.orders: n2 in the journal and n7 in the live graph. Only one can be live.
The live node keeps its id and the old node is folded into it, field by field. A field is filled from the journal only if no person has written that field on the live node. Anything a person wrote after the delete stays as they wrote it. Each field lands in one of three situations:
- Nobody wrote the field on the live node. It is filled from the journal. Example: the description of sales.orders.
- A person wrote a different value. The person's value is kept. The journal value is not applied and is listed in the report under not_restored. Example: owner ben instead of asha.
- A person emptied the field on purpose. It stays empty. This is why field_writes exists: an empty field that a person wrote is not the same as an empty field nobody touched. Example: the owner of the new sales.orders.email.
Description, owner and tags all follow this rule, and each one is treated as a whole value. For tags that means the two lists are never mixed: either the old list is filled in, or the person's list stays. Tags differ from the other two fields in one way only. They have a second layer, the inherited tags, and that layer is never filled or kept. It is recomputed. The last step of the usual case above shows every field of both merged nodes; the table below is the first of them.
All three situations are one rule: for each field, the value a person wrote most recently wins. Normally everything in the journal was written before the delete, and everything a person wrote on the live node came after it. So the person's value on the live node wins, and a field nobody touched is filled. The rule also settles the rare case where the journal holds the newer value, shown in the story "The recreated node is deleted again". A value that came with the seed counts as written at the very start. A value put back by an earlier undo counts from when a person first wrote it, not from when that undo ran. When the journal value wins over a value someone had written on the live node, the report lists the value it replaced under replaced, so nothing changes without showing up in the report.
type is not one of the three authored fields. It says what kind of thing the node is, such as table, view or column, and only ingest sets it. It follows the same idea with ingest as the writer: the type that ingest reported most recently wins. In a normal merge that is the type of the live node, and the report lists the old type when the two differ.

The old node is folded in. It is not brought back as a second node. Two live nodes cannot share a name, so a copy would need a different name, and the task's report has no outcome for that. A copy would also strand what undo is for: the description, owner and tags would sit on a node nobody uses, while the node that ingest keeps updating has none, and a tag such as pii would stop reaching the children. The cost is that the name is trusted. If a deleted name was reused for a different thing, the old values land on it. That is why only fields nobody wrote are filled, and why the report lists each one.
The live id stays because everything created after the delete already points at it: the arrows the ingest made, and any edit a person made. Every arrow that pointed at the old id is in the journal, so undo can re-aim those at the new id without touching anyone else's work. The mapping n2 → n7 is saved in removed_nodes.merged_into and used for the children and arrows that come after.
This gives mixed subtrees, and that is correct. sales.orders.total was not recreated, so it returns with its old id n4 under the new parent n7. The same rule applies whoever created the live node that holds the name. In this tool only ingest creates nodes. In the full system a person could also create one under an old name, and every field they filled in would be theirs and would stay.
### Arrows
For each removed arrow, undo first works out where each end is now: the same node if it is live, the node it was merged into if it was merged, or nowhere if it was skipped or deleted since.
- restored: both ends are live under their old ids. The arrow goes back as it was. Example: reports.daily → sales.orders.total.
- merged, reason endpoint_merged: one end was merged, so the arrow is put back pointing at the node that took over. Example: reports.daily → n2 becomes reports.daily → n7.
- merged, reason already_present: the same arrow already exists, because the ingest or a person made it. Nothing is added. Example: sales → n2 is already there as sales → n7.
- skipped, reason endpoint_not_live: one end is gone. Example: someone deleted reports.daily after the first delete. The row records which delete holds that node.
- skipped, reason child_has_other_parent: a contains arrow whose child now sits under a different parent. The later placement wins. Example: a person moved the new sales.orders under archive.
- skipped, reason removed_by_person: a person re-pointed this same arrow away after the delete. A re-point is two changes by that person, one arrow removed and one added, and undo keeps both. Example: a person moved the arrow of reports.daily from the new sales.orders to sales.refunds.
- skipped, reason would_create_cycle: a contains arrow that would make a node its own ancestor. Example: the ingest recreated two names with the parent and child swapped.
### When a later delete is in the way
The command is undo <op_id>. The person names the delete they want back, so nothing forces the newest delete to be undone first. If an older delete is undone while a newer one still stands, some of its rows may need a node that the newer delete removed.
- Such a row is skipped, with reason parent_not_live or endpoint_not_live. A node only disappears through a delete, so undo can always find which delete holds it. The row records that delete in waiting_on.
- When that later delete is undone, its undo first handles its own rows. Then it retries every row of earlier undos that waits on it, parents first, by the normal rules.
- A retried row keeps its single entry in the report of its own delete, with the outcome updated.
- Each retried row is its own step, so a crash during the retries is resumed like any other.
- Undone newest first, nothing ever waits.
The stories "A neighbour is deleted later" and "The parent is deleted later" show both cases.
### When inherited tags are worked out again
One rule covers every case: inherited tags are never taken from the journal. After each step, undo recomputes effective_tags for the node it touched and for everything below that node as the graph stands now, inside the same transaction. The cases this covers:
- A parent's tags changed while the node was deleted. A person added gdpr to sales after the delete. The restored sales.orders.total comes back carrying gdpr, which it never had before.
- A merge puts tags back on a node that has children now. pii returns to sales.orders (n7). It flows to the restored total, to the recreated email, and to currency, a column that was created after the delete and was never part of it.
- A person set tags on the recreated node. A person set the tags of the new sales.orders.email (n8) to ["hashed"]. Those stay and the old contact is not added back. Anything below n8 would inherit hashed, not contact. The report lists contact under not_restored, so a dropped tag is visible.
- The recreated node sits somewhere else. If n7 is under a different parent now, it stays there. The old children restored under it inherit from the new place, not the old one.
- A recreated node gets its old parent back. If n7 had no parent and the old contains arrow is put back onto it, n7 and its whole subtree are recomputed.
- A node is skipped. Nothing changes, so nothing is recomputed.
### Work done between the delete and the undo
Everything other people and the ingest did after the delete falls into one of three kinds. Each kind has one rule.
- Independent. It touched something the delete did not. Example: adding gdpr to sales, rewriting the description of sales.refunds, or creating currency. Rule: left exactly as it is. Restored nodes pick up its effects.
- Conflicting. It wrote something that undo would also write. Example: ben set the owner on the node that now holds the name sales.orders, and the journal says the owner was asha. The same goes for the new description and the new tags on sales.orders.email. Rule: the later human value wins, one field at a time. The old value is listed in the report and not applied.
- Caused. It happened only because the delete happened. Example: the ingest created n7 because no live node had that name. Rule: treat it as the same thing coming back. Fold the old node into it, keep the new id, re-aim the old arrows.
Undo only adds rows and fills fields that no person has written since the delete. It never overwrites or removes anything a person did after the delete.
The same holds for edits that arrive while undo is running. Each step reads the live graph inside its own transaction, so an edit that lands between two steps is handled exactly like one that landed before undo began.
### Crashes, resuming, and running it twice
- One step, one transaction. A step is one removed node or one removed arrow. Its graph change, its tag refresh and its outcome in the journal are saved together or not at all.
- Crash. With CRASH_AFTER=<n> set, undo counts every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE it runs. On the n-th one the process stops at once, without saving the step it is in, as a killed process would. SQLite discards the half-done step when the file is opened again. Steps that finished before it stay saved, so CRASH_AFTER=1 saves nothing: the first write is inside the first transaction. Only undo reads the variable.
- Resume. The next run skips every journal row that already has an outcome and carries on with the first one that does not. Each decision looks only at the live graph, so the resumed run makes the same decisions as an uninterrupted one.
- A dump in between. A node goes in before its arrows, and the database refuses an arrow to a missing node. A dump taken after a crash shows a smaller graph that is still whole, with correct tags.
- Run it twice. The second run finds an outcome on every row, writes nothing, and prints the same report.
### How long undo stays available
The rules above give a correct result however much time has passed. More edits only mean more rows come back as merged or skipped. What gets worse with time is how much of the result the person asking can predict.
The scenario gives one measured rate: several hundred edits in twenty minutes around a delete of 10,000 nodes. Taking 300 edits, that is 15 a minute.
 edits by others at the scenario's rate
 | time since the delete | edits by others | compared with the 10,000 deleted nodes
 | 20 minutes | 300 | 3%
 | 1 hour | 900 | 9%
 | 4 hours | 3,600 | 36%
 | 8 hours, one working day | 7,200 | 72%
 | about 11 hours | 10,000 | 100%
The last column is a ceiling. It assumes every edit lands on a different deleted node. At twenty minutes nearly everything comes back as it was. After about one working day of edits there are as many edits as deleted nodes. From there undo no longer takes back one action. It merges a day of other people's work with an old copy of 10,000 nodes, and the report is too long for a person to review.
The limit is 24 hours after the delete. A full day on the clock holds about one working day of edits, and it covers the usual late case: deleted in the evening, noticed the next morning. The value is subject to experimentation, because it rests on the one rate the scenario gives.
- Checked when undo starts. Undo compares the current time with the time the delete was applied, stored in ops. Past 24 hours it refuses, changes nothing, and says why. The journal rows stay where they are.
- An undo that has started can always finish. A crashed run is resumed and a finished run prints its report again, whatever the clock says. Otherwise a crash close to the limit would leave the graph half restored.
- The command-line tool does not enforce it. The task puts retention out of scope, the operations in the fixture carry no real clock, and the checks expect undo to run on the fixture whenever it is called. The limit belongs to the full system.

## 4How redo works
Redo is the one extension the task names. This section is its design. The tool's four commands do not include it yet, but undo already records everything redo needs.
redo <op_id> takes the op_id of a subtree delete that has been undone, and applies the delete again to the graph as it is now. It does not replay the delete from scratch. It takes back what the undo put back: restored nodes go out again, the arrows undo added are removed, and the fields undo filled get the value they had before. Like undo, it never removes or changes anything a person did in the meantime. For redo, "in the meantime" means after the undo.
Pick a story, then step through it. Each one starts where an undo left the graph.

### What redo does, in order
- Take every row that the undo of this delete decided. That is the delete's own rows, plus any rows of earlier deletes that this undo retried.
- Take the nodes undo restored, children before parents. For each one decide removed or kept (next figure). A removed node goes back into the journal together with every arrow that touches it. That is one transaction.
- For each node undo merged, put back the fields undo filled, then refresh the tags of the live node and everything below it.
- Take the remaining arrows undo added, the ones between nodes that stay, and remove them.
- Record the redo as an operation of its own and print the report.
The order is undo's order turned around. Undo goes parents first, because a child needs its parent to attach to. Redo goes children first, because a parent can only leave once nothing is left under it.

A node leaves only when it is exactly as undo left it and nothing else depends on it. Because children are handled first, a parent whose child was kept is kept too.
### Taking a restored node out again
A node undo restored is removed again when both of these hold. Otherwise it is kept, and the report gives the reason.
- No person has written it since it came back. field_writes holds the number of the last write to each field, and the undo has a number of its own in ops. A write by a person with a larger number came after the undo. Reason when it fails: written_since_undo.
- Nothing else is attached to it. Every child and every arrow that touches it must be one this redo is taking out as well. A node created or moved under it since, an arrow a person or the ingest added to it since, a child that was itself kept, or something another undo put there, all keep it in place. Reason: still_in_use.
A removed node goes back into the journal of its delete, and its name is free again. The journal copy is refreshed from the live node as it leaves. If the ingest reported a new type for the node while it was back, that type is not lost. A write by the ingest does not keep a node in place: it only happened because the node was there, and the next ingest run recreates the node if the source still has it.
What a row goes back to depends on whose row it is:
- A row of this delete has no outcome again, as it was right after the delete. So undo can run again later and decides the row afresh against the graph of that moment.
- A row of an earlier delete that this undo retried goes back to skipped, waiting_on this delete. That is what it was before the undo.
### Putting filled fields back
When undo merged an old node into a live one, it filled some fields of the live node and saved what they held before in prior: the value, and who wrote it and when. Redo goes through the filled fields one at a time:
- The field is still as undo left it. Redo puts back the earlier value and the earlier write record. Most of the time the earlier value is "empty, nobody wrote it". Example: the description and the tag pii on the new sales.orders.
- A person has written the field since the undo. It stays as the person wrote it. Reason: written_since_undo.
Undo copied the old write record along with the value, so "still as undo left it" is a plain comparison: the field's write record is still the one undo copied. Fields undo did not fill were never touched and are not touched now. Inherited tags are recomputed, as always: when pii leaves the live node, it leaves everything below it.
### Arrows
- removed: undo added the arrow, and it goes out again. This covers an arrow that touches a removed node, and an arrow undo re-aimed at a node that stays. Example: reports.daily → n7.
- kept, reason end_kept: the arrow touches a restored node that redo kept. A node that stays keeps the arrows undo gave it, so it is not left half connected.
- unchanged, reason not_added_by_undo: undo found the arrow already there, or skipped it. There is nothing to take back.
- unchanged, reason changed_since_undo: someone re-pointed the arrow away after the undo. Whether it is there now or not is their doing, so redo leaves it as it is.
### Work done between the undo and the redo
The same three kinds as for undo, each with one rule.
- Independent. It touched something undo did not put back. Rule: left exactly as it is.
- Conflicting. A person wrote on, or attached something to, a thing undo put back. Example: a person rewrote the description of the restored sales.orders.total. Rule: that thing stays, with everything it needs to stay whole: its parents and its arrows. The report lists it as kept.
- Caused. It happened only because the undo happened. Example: the ingest found sales.orders.total live again and updated its type instead of creating a new node. Rule: it does not hold redo back, and the journal copy keeps the newer type.
Redo only takes back rows undo decided, and only while they are as undo left them. It never overwrites or removes anything a person did after the undo.
### Redo, undo, and their order
- Redo straight after undo gives back the graph from before the undo. Nothing has changed in between, so every row is taken back. The dump is the same, byte for byte, as the dump taken just before the undo.
- Undo can run again after a redo. The rows redo took back have no outcome, so undo decides them like new rows. With nothing changed in between, it gives the same graph as the first undo.
- Only an undone delete can be redone. For a delete that was never undone, for any other operation, or for an id that does not exist, redo prints an error and writes nothing.
- After several undos, redo the newest undo first. If an older undo is redone while a newer one still stands, some of its nodes may carry arrows or children the newer undo put there. Those nodes are kept, reason still_in_use. Redone newest first, nothing is kept for this reason. This mirrors undo, where the newest delete undone first means nothing waits.
- Each round has its own entry in ops. The first undo of d1 is undo:d1 and its redo is redo:d1. A second round is undo:d1:2 and redo:d1:2. Every row names the undo that decided it, so "since it came back" always has an exact meaning.
### Crashes and running it twice
- One row, one transaction, as for undo. The graph change, the tag refresh and the row's redo outcome are saved together or not at all.
- Each journal row gets a redo outcome next to its undo outcome: removed, kept or unchanged for nodes and arrows, and reverted for a merged node, with a reason. The report is a printout of those.
- Crash and resume. CRASH_AFTER=<n> works for redo as it does for undo. A resumed run skips every row that already has a redo outcome.
- Run it twice. The second run finds a redo outcome on every row, writes nothing, and prints the same report.

### What the checker would test
- No change made by a person after the undo is lost or altered by the redo. Tested like check 1, with a dump just before the redo and one just after.
- Redo straight after undo gives the dump from before the undo, byte for byte. A second undo then gives the dump from after the first undo.
- The report accounts for every row the undo decided, exactly once, and each outcome agrees with the dump: a removed row is gone, a kept row is there, a reverted field holds its earlier value.
- The graph stays whole. No two live nodes share a name, no arrow points at a missing node, and inherited tags are correct.
- Redo is idempotent and resumable, tested as checks 6 and 7 are for undo.
Each redo story above becomes a test in the small fixture, the same way the undo stories did.
## The eight checks and what makes each one hold
- No human change after the delete is lost. Undo only inserts rows and fills fields with no human write since the delete, read from field_writes. The checker proves it by comparing a dump taken just before undo with the dump taken after: every value a person wrote is unchanged, every arrow a person added is still there, and no arrow a person moved away has come back.
- Free name and live parent means restored. This is the node decision in the figure above. The task says the parent must be live "at undo time". Here that means: live once undo has dealt with the parent, whether the parent was restored or was merged into the node that holds its name. The checker uses the same reading. From its own replay it works out which removed names are free and which parents are live, and expects each such node in the dump after undo with its old id, description, owner and tags.
- No two live nodes share a name. A clash becomes a merge before any insert, and the UNIQUE rule on the table backs it up. The checker counts the names in the dump after undo.
- The report covers every removed node and arrow once. The report is a printout of the journal rows of that delete. Each row has exactly one outcome. The checker builds the list of removed nodes and arrows from its own replay and matches it against the report: nothing missing, nothing twice. It also holds each outcome against the dump: a restored row is there under its old id, a merged row points at a live node, a skipped row is absent.
- Inherited tags are correct. They are recomputed from the live graph inside every step. The checker recomputes them from the own tags and the contains arrows in the dump, and compares.
- Running undo twice gives the same dump. The second run has no row left to decide, so it writes nothing. The run script runs undo again, and the checker expects the same dump and the same report, byte for byte.
- A crashed undo can be finished. One transaction per step, and foreign keys rule out arrows to missing nodes. The task does not say which n, so it has to hold for any. The run script copies the database after apply and runs a clean undo on one copy and crashed undos on others: at the first write, at a few in the middle, at the last, at a number larger than the total, and with two and three crashes in a row. The checker compares what they left.
- Under 60 seconds. The scenario is about 5,000 rows and a few thousand small transactions. The run script times the scenario and the whole run, and the checker fails if either goes over. The work grows in step with the number of removed rows, one small transaction each, so the 10,000-node case follows the same path.
## The fixture
The fixture is the test data. gen_fixture.py writes it from a seed number, and the same seed always gives the same files.
seed.jsonl
The starting graph: about 5,000 nodes and edges.
ops.jsonl
The operations, in order. First, one subtree delete of at least 500 nodes. Then about 300 operations of mixed kinds.
planted.json
Which nodes each planted case below uses, so the checker can find each case and test it. The eight checks do not use it.
One line of each kind, with ids shortened:
# seed.jsonl
{"kind": "node", "id": "n2", "qualified_name": "sales.orders", "type": "table", "description": "One row per order", "owner": "asha", "tags": ["pii"]}
{"kind": "edge", "from_id": "n1", "to_id": "n2", "type": "contains"}
# ops.jsonl
{"op_id": "d1", "actor": "human", "kind": "delete_subtree", "root_id": "n2"}
{"op_id": "op17", "actor": "ingest", "kind": "ingest_node", "qualified_name": "sales.orders", "type": "table", "parent": "sales"}
{"op_id": "op31", "actor": "human", "kind": "edit_node", "id": "n7", "set": {"owner": "ben"}}
{"op_id": "op40", "actor": "human", "kind": "add_edge", "from_id": "n6", "to_id": "n5", "type": "references"}
{"op_id": "op52", "actor": "human", "kind": "repoint_edge", "from_id": "n6", "to_id": "n7", "type": "references", "new_to_id": "n5"}
The seed holds no inherited tags. They are worked out when the seed is loaded. An ingest line carries no id, because the tool makes it. Since that id follows from the op_id and the name, the generator can work it out too and use it in later lines, as op31 does with n7.
The task sets minimums for those operations. After writing the files the generator counts each one, prints the counts, and stops with an error if any is not met:
- The delete removes at least 500 nodes.
- People edit nodes next to the deleted area: its parent, its siblings, and nodes that referenced it.
- Edges are re-pointed to other nodes.
- An ingest run recreates at least 50 of the deleted names under new ids.
- People edit at least 5 of those recreated nodes.
Random data alone might never reach a rare rule, so the generator also plants one case for each of these:
- A recreated node that nobody edited. Its three fields are filled from the journal.
- A recreated node where a person changed a field. The person's value is kept.
- A recreated node where a person emptied a field. It stays empty.
- A recreated node that a person moved under another parent. The old parent arrow is skipped.
- A deleted name that was not recreated, under a parent that was. It is restored with its old id under the new parent.
- A recreated child whose parent name was not recreated. It gets its old parent back.
- A reference that a person re-pointed onto a recreated node. The old arrow is counted as already present.
- A reference that a person re-pointed away from a recreated node. The old arrow is skipped.
- A recreated node whose type differs from the old one. The newer type stays and the report lists the old one.
- A tag that a person added above the deleted root. Restored nodes come back carrying it.
### The second, small fixture
The task's scenario has one subtree delete, so it never reaches the rules for two deletes. A second, small set of test data covers them. It is the six-node graph from the stories above, with one operations file per story, so each story is also the description of a test.
seed.jsonl
The six nodes and six arrows the stories start from.
ops_a.jsonl
Story "A neighbour is deleted later". d1 deletes sales.orders, then d2 deletes reports.daily.
ops_b.jsonl
Story "The parent is deleted later". d1 deletes sales.orders, then d2 deletes sales.
ops_c.jsonl
Story "The recreated node is deleted again". d1 deletes sales.orders. Ingest recreates it as a view. A person sets its owner to ben. d2 deletes the recreated node.
ops_d.jsonl
Story "The usual case". d1 deletes sales.orders. A person adds gdpr to sales and rewrites the description of sales.refunds. Ingest recreates sales.orders and sales.orders.email and adds sales.orders.currency. People edit the two recreated nodes as in the story.
ops_e.jsonl
Story "A person moved an arrow away". d1 deletes sales.orders. Ingest recreates it and its arrow from reports.daily. A person re-points that arrow to sales.refunds.
ops_f.jsonl
Story "The recreated node was moved". People do not create nodes, so first the ingest creates archive and a person gives it the tag old. d1 deletes sales.orders, ingest recreates it, and a person moves it under archive.
The content is fixed, with no random choices. gen_fixture.py --small writes the seven files. Files a, b and c have two deletes. Each is run twice from a fresh load: once undoing d1 and then d2, and once undoing d2 and then d1. Files d, e and f have one delete and are run once. That makes nine runs. The checker tests each one for:
- Files d, e and f. The report of undo d1 is the one the story shows, and the graph ends as the story's last picture. For file d that report is the example report above, word for word.
- Files a and b, both orders. After both undos the dump is the same, byte for byte, as the dump taken right after load. Everything that was deleted is back and nothing else changed.
- Files a and b, d1 undone first. After the first undo the blocked rows are skipped and name d2 in waiting_on. After the second undo, the report of d1 shows them restored.
- File c, both orders. One live sales.orders, owner ben, type view, the old description and the tag pii, with sales.orders.total under it. The two orders differ in one thing only: the node that came back first keeps its id.
- Every undo in every run. The checks that do not depend on the big scenario: no human change lost, no shared name, every removed row in the report once, inherited tags correct, and a second call that changes nothing.
## What the repository holds
README.md
The exact commands to generate the fixture, run the scenario and run the checker.
DECISIONS.md
One page. The rule chosen for independent, conflicting and caused edits. What the model proposed that was rejected, and why. What was verified by hand.
AI sessions
Every AI session used for the work, complete and unedited, as a share link, an exported transcript or a log file. A session from a tool that cannot export is described in DECISIONS.md.
### The scenario, in order
python gen_fixture.py --seed 7 --out fixture
python graphundo.py load fixture/seed.jsonl
python graphundo.py apply fixture/ops.jsonl
python graphundo.py dump > before.jsonl
python graphundo.py undo <op_id of the delete> > report.json
python graphundo.py dump > after.jsonl
python checker.py fixture before.jsonl after.jsonl report.json
The dump before undo is there for check 1. "No human change is lost" can only be shown by holding what people had written just before undo against what is there just after. A run script wraps these commands. It then calls undo a second time for check 6, repeats the run with CRASH_AFTER set for check 7, times the whole thing for check 8, and then runs the nine runs of the small second fixture. On the three files above the checker runs the checks that need only one undo. The checker never runs the tool itself; for checks 6, 7 and 8 it reads what the run script saved:
python run_scenario.py --fixture fixture --small fixture_small --out run
python checker.py fixture --small fixture_small --run run

# Decisions

Undo does not roll the graph back. It applies the inverse of one delete to the graph as it is now: it
only adds rows and fills fields, and never removes a row or replaces a value a person wrote after the
delete.

## Conflict rules

**Independent edits** touched something the delete did not, such as the deleted root's parent or
siblings, a dashboard that pointed into the deleted area, or a node created elsewhere. Rule: undo leaves
them exactly as they are, and restored nodes pick up their effects. A tag a person added above the
deleted root flows into every restored node below it.

**Conflicting edits** wrote a field that undo would also write. Rule: for each field, the most recent
write wins.
- The seed counts as written at the start.
- A value put back by an undo keeps the time of its original write.
- Everything in the journal was written before the delete, so a value a person wrote after the delete
  always wins. The journal value is then listed under `not_restored`.
- A field nobody wrote is filled from the journal.
- A field a person emptied on purpose stays empty. `field_writes` tells it apart from a field nobody wrote.
- Tags count as one value: the two lists are never mixed.
- `effective_tags` is never copied back. Undo recomputes it from the live graph in every step.
- `type` follows the same rule, with ingest as the writer.

**Caused edits** only happened because the delete did. The typical case: the ingest found a name free
and created a new node with a new id. Rule: undo treats it as the same thing coming back. It merges the
old node into the live one, keeps the live id (everything made since already points at it), and re-aims
the old arrows at it.

## The decisions undo makes

For each removed node, parents first, one transaction per node:
- Its name is held by a live node: **merged** into that node.
- Otherwise its parent is live, or was merged: **restored** with its old id and all its fields.
- Otherwise: **skipped** (`parent_not_live`). `waiting_on` names the delete that holds the parent.

For each removed arrow, after resolving each end to where it is now. The first match wins:
1. An end is not live: skipped (`endpoint_not_live`), waiting on that end's delete.
2. The arrow already exists: merged (`already_present`).
3. It is a contains arrow and the child already has a parent: skipped (`child_has_other_parent`).
   The later placement wins.
4. A person re-pointed this arrow away after the delete: skipped (`removed_by_person`).
5. It would make a node its own ancestor: skipped (`would_create_cycle`).
6. Otherwise it is added: restored, or merged (`endpoint_merged`) when an end was merged.

Undoing a later delete retries the rows that were waiting on it: newest journal first, then parents
first. In this order nothing has to wait. A row that already has an outcome is never decided again.
That makes a second run write nothing, and a crashed run resume from its last committed step.

## What the model proposed that I rejected, and why

Design:
- **Several parents per node**, offered as a fix for a "conflict" with the task. I had it re-read the
  task: "subtree", "root" and "its parent" describe a tree, so one parent per node stayed.
- **Fixing the design page before showing me the problems.** I stopped it before any edit landed,
  had it list the problems first, and approved every change one by one after that.
- **A wrong example** of undo reversing a person's re-point (an arrow to a deleted node is deleted
  too). It corrected it when I asked for the steps, and I chose the rule that undo skips an arrow a
  person moved away.
- **Invariant 2 as a problem.** Undo brings back parent and child, so only the reading of "parent is
  live" needed one line.
- **Handling edits to deleted nodes.** The task does not ask for it; it stays one "rejected" sentence.
- **A preview before undo:** good UX, not core capability for a prototype.

Build:
- **Choices that bent the task's wording**, found when I had every deviation checked against it:
  WAL mode (extra files beside "one SQLite file"), dropping repeated tags ("tags (a list)"), and
  skipping the tag recompute after a delete. All three were put back.
- **Refusing operations by the "wrong" actor**, beyond the task's one rule. Only two refusals remain:
  ingest can't edit fields, and people can't ingest.
- **Silently skipping an op_id that was already used**, even for a different operation. Now an error.
- **The 24-hour undo limit**, my own idea: I had it enforced, then removed it, because the task says
  any delete can be undone later and puts retention out of scope.

I also weighed keeping a duplicate node instead of merging, and kept merging: invariant 3 allows one
live node per name, and the task's outcomes include "merged".

## What I verified myself

- **The design, after every iteration.** I reviewed the whole page each time it changed, and read
  every audit against the task point by point, accepting, rejecting or questioning each one myself.
- **The undo stories.** I stepped through the undo tabs, asked for the other fields' clashes beside
  tags, and asked for every exceptional case to become a story of its own, start to end. Those stories
  are now tests (`fixture_small/ops_a` to `ops_f`).
- **Claims against the task's wording.** I made the model re-check several before accepting them:
  several parents, undo of anything but a delete, only ingest creating nodes, ids built from op_id and
  name, edits to deleted nodes.
- **The code against the task and the design.** I had every deviation listed, decided each one, and
  had duplicated code removed with outputs proven byte-identical before and after.

1	# Undo in a shared graph
2	
3	A command-line tool that keeps a graph of entities and relationships in one SQLite file, and can undo a
4	subtree delete after other people and an ingest job have kept editing the graph. Instead of rolling the
5	graph back, undo puts back what the delete removed on top of the graph as it is now. For every removed
6	node and arrow it reports one outcome: restored, merged or skipped. The rules it follows are in
7	[DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md), and the full design, with step-by-step stories, is in
8	[docs/design.html](docs/design.html) (download it and open it in a browser).
9	
10	Python 3.11 or newer. Nothing to install: everything comes from the standard library.
11	
12	## Run it
13	
14	```bash
15	python3 gen_fixture.py --seed 7 --out fixture
16	python3 gen_fixture.py --small --out fixture_small
17	python3 run_scenario.py --fixture fixture --small fixture_small --out run
18	python3 checker.py fixture --small fixture_small --run run
19	```
20	
21	1. Writes `fixture/seed.jsonl` (1,717 nodes and 3,034 arrows), `fixture/ops.jsonl` (one delete of 620
22	   nodes, then 300 operations) and `fixture/planted.json`. Prints the counts the task asks for and stops
23	   with an error, writing nothing, if one is missed. Same seed, same files.
24	2. Writes the six-node fixture from the design's stories: `seed.jsonl` and one operations file per
25	   story, `ops_a.jsonl` to `ops_f.jsonl`.
26	3. Runs the tool as a subprocess and saves every dump and report under `run/`. The main scenario is
27	   load, apply, dump, undo, dump (timed). Then it runs undo a second time, and runs 11 crashed undos on
28	   copies of the database taken right after apply. On another copy it applies the operations file
29	   again, then a file that re-uses an op_id for a different operation. Last, it runs each story's file
30	   from a fresh load, the two-delete ones in both undo orders. Takes about 7 seconds.
31	4. Reads only files and never runs the tool. Prints one PASS or FAIL line per check, and exits with
32	   status 0 when every check passes.
33	
34	Optional: `python3 mutation_check.py` breaks the undo in 9 different ways, each in a throwaway copy of
35	the repository, and shows which checks catch each break. It takes about a minute and exits with status 0
36	when every break is caught.
37	
38	## The scenario by hand
39	
40	```bash
41	python3 graphundo.py load fixture/seed.jsonl
42	python3 graphundo.py apply fixture/ops.jsonl
43	python3 graphundo.py dump > before.jsonl
44	python3 graphundo.py undo op0001 > report.json
45	python3 graphundo.py dump > after.jsonl
46	python3 checker.py fixture before.jsonl after.jsonl report.json
47	```
48	
49	The delete is the first operation, `op0001`. The database is `graph.db` in the current directory. Use
50	`--db PATH` or `GRAPHUNDO_DB` to put it somewhere else. On these three files the checker runs checks 0 to
51	5 and the planted cases. Checks 6, 7 and 8 need the extra runs that `run_scenario.py` makes.
52	
53	A crash and a resume, on a database where the delete has not been undone yet:
54	
55	```bash
56	CRASH_AFTER=500 python3 graphundo.py undo op0001    # stops after 500 writes, exit status 3
57	python3 graphundo.py dump                           # a smaller graph, still whole, tags correct
58	python3 graphundo.py undo op0001                    # carries on: same final dump and report
59	```
60	
61	`CRASH_AFTER=n` kills the process right after its n-th write, the way a crash would. Steps that finished
62	before it stay saved. The step it was in the middle of is rolled back by SQLite the next time the file is
63	opened. So `CRASH_AFTER=1` saves nothing: the first write is inside the first transaction.
64	
65	## Commands
66	
67	- `load SEED`: creates a new database from the seed, replacing an old one. The seed is checked first:
68	  ids are UUIDs, ids and names are unique, every arrow joins two seed nodes, no node has two parents and
69	  there is no loop. `effective_tags` is worked out for the whole graph.
70	- `apply OPS`: applies the operations in order, one transaction each. An operation that cannot be applied
71	  as written is stored as rejected, with its reason, and changes nothing. An op_id names one operation:
72	  running apply again on the same file skips what is already there, and an op_id that was already used
73	  for a different operation stops apply with an error before anything changes.
74	- `undo OP_ID`: undoes one `delete_subtree` and prints the report. Any other op_id prints an error and
75	  writes nothing. It reads `CRASH_AFTER=<n>`. On stderr it says how many writes it made. The undo is
76	  logged in `ops` as an operation of its own (`undo:<op_id>`, by a person). Every journal row records
77	  which undo decided it, and a merge records what the live node held before. That is what a redo needs.
78	- `dump`: prints the live graph as JSONL. Node lines come first, sorted by id. Arrow lines follow, sorted
79	  by from_id, to_id and type. Equal graphs print the same bytes.
80	
81	## Input files
82	
83	```json
84	{"kind": "node", "id": "…uuid…", "qualified_name": "warehouse.sales.orders", "type": "table", "description": "Orders in sales", "owner": "asha", "tags": ["pii"]}
85	{"kind": "edge", "from_id": "…", "to_id": "…", "type": "contains"}
86	```
87	
88	Each operation line has `op_id`, `actor` (`human` or `ingest`) and `kind`:
89	
90	```json
91	{"op_id": "op0001", "actor": "human",  "kind": "delete_subtree", "root_id": "…"}
92	{"op_id": "op0002", "actor": "human",  "kind": "edit_node", "id": "…", "set": {"owner": "ben", "tags": ["pii"]}}
93	{"op_id": "op0003", "actor": "human",  "kind": "add_edge", "from_id": "…", "to_id": "…", "type": "references"}
94	{"op_id": "op0004", "actor": "human",  "kind": "repoint_edge", "from_id": "…", "to_id": "…", "type": "references", "new_to_id": "…"}
95	{"op_id": "op0005", "actor": "ingest", "kind": "ingest_node", "qualified_name": "warehouse.sales.orders", "type": "table", "parent": "warehouse.sales"}
96	```
97	
98	- `repoint_edge` takes exactly one of `new_from_id` and `new_to_id`. Re-pointing a contains arrow's
99	  `from_id` moves a node under another parent.
100	- `ingest_node` updates the type of the live node that has the name. When no live node has the name, it
101	  creates one under `parent`, if that parent is live, and at the top level otherwise. The new node's id is
102	  `uuid5(2f0c9a52-8a4e-4c55-9d1b-1b0f6d1e7a3c, "<op_id>/<qualified_name>")`, so later operations in the
103	  same file can refer to it. Ingest never sets description, owner or tags.
104	- Who did an operation matters twice. An `edit_node` from ingest is refused, because ingest never sets
105	  description, owner or tags. An `ingest_node` from a person is refused, because people do not create
106	  nodes. `add_edge`, `repoint_edge` and `delete_subtree` can come from either.
107	
108	## The report
109	
110	```json
111	{
112	  "op_id": "op0001",
113	  "summary": {"nodes": {"restored": 547, "merged": 73, "skipped": 0}, "edges": {"restored": 531, "merged": 497, "skipped": 4}},
114	  "nodes": [

# Undo in a shared graph

A command-line tool that keeps a graph of entities and relationships in one SQLite file, and can undo a
subtree delete after other people and an ingest job have kept editing the graph. Instead of rolling the
graph back, undo puts back what the delete removed on top of the graph as it is now. For every removed
node and arrow it reports one outcome: restored, merged or skipped. The rules it follows are in
[DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md), and the full design, with step-by-step stories, is in
[docs/design.html](docs/design.html) (download it and open it in a browser).

Python 3.11 or newer. Nothing to install: everything comes from the standard library.

## Run it

```bash
python3 gen_fixture.py --seed 7 --out fixture
python3 gen_fixture.py --small --out fixture_small
python3 run_scenario.py --fixture fixture --small fixture_small --out run
python3 checker.py fixture --small fixture_small --run run
```

1. Writes `fixture/seed.jsonl` (1,717 nodes and 3,034 arrows), `fixture/ops.jsonl` (one delete of 620
   nodes, then 300 operations) and `fixture/planted.json`. Prints the counts the task asks for and stops
   with an error, writing nothing, if one is missed. Same seed, same files.
2. Writes the six-node fixture from the design's stories: `seed.jsonl` and one operations file per
   story, `ops_a.jsonl` to `ops_f.jsonl`.
3. Runs the tool as a subprocess and saves every dump and report under `run/`. The main scenario is
   load, apply, dump, undo, dump (timed). Then it runs undo a second time, and runs 11 crashed undos on
   copies of the database taken right after apply. On another copy it applies the operations file
   again, then a file that re-uses an op_id for a different operation. Last, it runs each story's file
   from a fresh load, the two-delete ones in both undo orders. Takes about 7 seconds.
4. Reads only files and never runs the tool. Prints one PASS or FAIL line per check, and exits with
   status 0 when every check passes.

Optional: `python3 mutation_check.py` breaks the undo in 9 different ways, each in a throwaway copy of
the repository, and shows which checks catch each break. It takes about a minute and exits with status 0
when every break is caught.

## The scenario by hand

```bash
python3 graphundo.py load fixture/seed.jsonl
python3 graphundo.py apply fixture/ops.jsonl
python3 graphundo.py dump > before.jsonl
python3 graphundo.py undo op0001 > report.json
python3 graphundo.py dump > after.jsonl
python3 checker.py fixture before.jsonl after.jsonl report.json
```

The delete is the first operation, `op0001`. The database is `graph.db` in the current directory. Use
`--db PATH` or `GRAPHUNDO_DB` to put it somewhere else. On these three files the checker runs checks 0 to
5 and the planted cases. Checks 6, 7 and 8 need the extra runs that `run_scenario.py` makes.

A crash and a resume, on a database where the delete has not been undone yet:

```bash
CRASH_AFTER=500 python3 graphundo.py undo op0001    # stops after 500 writes, exit status 3
python3 graphundo.py dump                           # a smaller graph, still whole, tags correct
python3 graphundo.py undo op0001                    # carries on: same final dump and report
```

`CRASH_AFTER=n` kills the process right after its n-th write, the way a crash would. Steps that finished
before it stay saved. The step it was in the middle of is rolled back by SQLite the next time the file is
opened. So `CRASH_AFTER=1` saves nothing: the first write is inside the first transaction.

## Commands

- `load SEED`: creates a new database from the seed, replacing an old one. The seed is checked first:
  ids are UUIDs, ids and names are unique, every arrow joins two seed nodes, no node has two parents and
  there is no loop. `effective_tags` is worked out for the whole graph.
- `apply OPS`: applies the operations in order, one transaction each. An operation that cannot be applied
  as written is stored as rejected, with its reason, and changes nothing. An op_id names one operation:
  running apply again on the same file skips what is already there, and an op_id that was already used
  for a different operation stops apply with an error before anything changes.
- `undo OP_ID`: undoes one `delete_subtree` and prints the report. Any other op_id prints an error and
  writes nothing. It reads `CRASH_AFTER=<n>`. On stderr it says how many writes it made. The undo is
  logged in `ops` as an operation of its own (`undo:<op_id>`, by a person). Every journal row records
  which undo decided it, and a merge records what the live node held before. That is what a redo needs.
- `dump`: prints the live graph as JSONL. Node lines come first, sorted by id. Arrow lines follow, sorted
  by from_id, to_id and type. Equal graphs print the same bytes.

## Input files

```json
{"kind": "node", "id": "…uuid…", "qualified_name": "warehouse.sales.orders", "type": "table", "description": "Orders in sales", "owner": "asha", "tags": ["pii"]}
{"kind": "edge", "from_id": "…", "to_id": "…", "type": "contains"}
```

Each operation line has `op_id`, `actor` (`human` or `ingest`) and `kind`:

```json
{"op_id": "op0001", "actor": "human",  "kind": "delete_subtree", "root_id": "…"}
{"op_id": "op0002", "actor": "human",  "kind": "edit_node", "id": "…", "set": {"owner": "ben", "tags": ["pii"]}}
{"op_id": "op0003", "actor": "human",  "kind": "add_edge", "from_id": "…", "to_id": "…", "type": "references"}
{"op_id": "op0004", "actor": "human",  "kind": "repoint_edge", "from_id": "…", "to_id": "…", "type": "references", "new_to_id": "…"}
{"op_id": "op0005", "actor": "ingest", "kind": "ingest_node", "qualified_name": "warehouse.sales.orders", "type": "table", "parent": "warehouse.sales"}
```

- `repoint_edge` takes exactly one of `new_from_id` and `new_to_id`. Re-pointing a contains arrow's
  `from_id` moves a node under another parent.
- `ingest_node` updates the type of the live node that has the name. When no live node has the name, it
  creates one under `parent`, if that parent is live, and at the top level otherwise. The new node's id is
  `uuid5(2f0c9a52-8a4e-4c55-9d1b-1b0f6d1e7a3c, "<op_id>/<qualified_name>")`, so later operations in the
  same file can refer to it. Ingest never sets description, owner or tags.
- Who did an operation matters twice. An `edit_node` from ingest is refused, because ingest never sets
  description, owner or tags. An `ingest_node` from a person is refused, because people do not create
  nodes. `add_edge`, `repoint_edge` and `delete_subtree` can come from either.

## The report

```json
{
  "op_id": "op0001",
  "summary": {"nodes": {"restored": 547, "merged": 73, "skipped": 0}, "edges": {"restored": 531, "merged": 497, "skipped": 4}},
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "…", "qualified_name": "warehouse.sales.employees", "outcome": "merged", "reason": "name_in_use", "merged_into": "…", "filled": ["description", "tags"], "kept_live": ["owner"], "not_restored": {"owner": "jo"}},
    {"id": "…", "qualified_name": "warehouse.sales.invoices", "outcome": "restored"}
  ],
  "edges": [
    {"from": "…", "to": "…", "type": "references", "outcome": "skipped", "reason": "removed_by_person", "now": ["…", "…"]}
  ]
}
```

The report has one entry for every node and arrow the delete removed, in parents-first order. `merged`
and `skipped` entries always carry a reason. A merged node lists the fields filled from the journal,
the fields that kept their live value, and the old values that were not applied. When a filled value
replaced one that someone had written on the live node, `replaced` shows what was there. A merged or skipped
arrow shows where its ends are now (`now`). A row blocked by a later delete names that delete in
`waiting_on`. Undoing that delete retries the row, and the next printout of this report shows the new
outcome.

## What the checker checks

The checker imports nothing from the tool. It replays the seed and the operations in plain dictionaries
(`replay.py`, its own copy of the operation rules), then compares the replay with the saved dumps and
reports.

- **0** The dump before undo equals the replayed graph, so apply did what the operations say.
- **1** Nothing a person did after the delete is lost: the fields they wrote, the arrows they added,
  the arrows they moved away and the nodes they deleted are all as they were just before undo.
- **2** Every removed node whose name is free, and whose parent is live or merged, is back under its
  old id with its description, owner and tags.
- **3** No two live nodes share a qualified_name.
- **4** The report lists every removed node and arrow exactly once, and each outcome matches the dump.
  A restored row is live, a merged row's target is live under the same name, and a skipped row is absent.
  A merged row's kept fields are unchanged, its filled fields hold the journal value, and `replaced` is
  what the target held before.
- **5** `effective_tags` recomputed from the dump matches, and no arrow points at a missing node.
- **6** A second undo gives the same dump and the same report, byte for byte, and writes nothing.
- **7** Crashed undos (CRASH_AFTER = the first write, a few in the middle, the last, past the end, two
  and three crashes in a row) finish with the same dump and report as a clean run. A dump between runs
  has no arrow to a missing node, has correct tags and has unique names.
- **8** Load, apply, dump, undo and dump take under 60 seconds (about 1.5 seconds), and so does the whole
  run with every extra undo (about 7 seconds).

It also checks the 11 cases the generator planted (`planted.json`). Applying the operations file again
changes nothing, and an op_id re-used for another operation is refused without changing anything. For
the nine small runs, one per story of the design:
- **Files a and b.** Undoing both deletes gives back the dump right after load, byte for byte. Rows
  blocked by d2 wait on d2, and come back when d2 is undone.
- **File c.** It ends with one `sales.orders` owned by ben, of type view, with the old description and
  tags. The two undo orders differ only in which id survives.
- **Files d, e and f.** The report and the end state are the ones the story shows. For d, the report is
  the design's example report, word for word.

## Repository

- `graphundo.py`: the command-line entry point.
- `graph_undo/store.py`: async access to SQLite. Every sqlite3 call runs on one worker thread behind
  an async API, so the event loop never blocks on the disk. It counts writes for CRASH_AFTER.
- `graph_undo/schema.py`: the live tables (`nodes`, `edges`) and the journal (`ops`, `field_writes`,
  `edge_removals`, `removed_nodes`, `removed_edges`).
- `graph_undo/graph.py`: the reads and writes that apply, undo and the tag propagator share, on the
  live graph and the operation log.
- `graph_undo/loader.py`, `applier.py`, `tags.py`, `undo.py`, `dumper.py`, `cli.py`: load, apply, the
  tag propagator, undo, dump and the command line.
- `replay.py`: the operations applied to plain dictionaries. The checker holds the tool against it.
  The generator applies each operation it writes to it, so every operation is valid when it runs.
- `gen_fixture.py`, `run_scenario.py`, `checker.py`, `mutation_check.py`: test data, harness, checker,
  and the checker's own test.

The database is one SQLite file in SQLite's default rollback-journal mode. While a transaction runs,
SQLite keeps a journal next to it. A crash can leave that journal behind, and the next command that
opens the database rolls the unfinished step back. `load` builds the new database as
`graph.db.loading` and renames it to `graph.db` at the end, so a load that fails leaves the old
database as it was.

  • Nothing else is attached to it. Every child and every arrow that touches it must be one this redo is taking out as well. A node created or moved under it since, an arrow a person or the ingest added to 628:

    When undo merged an old node into a live one, it filled some fields of the live node and saved what they held before in prior: the value, and who wrote it and when. Redo goes through the filled fiel 630:

  • The field is still as undo left it. Redo puts back the earlier value and the earlier write record. Most of the time the earlier value is "empty, nobody wrote it". Example: the description and the tag < 638:

  • unchanged, reason changed_since_undo: someone re-pointed the arrow away after the undo. Whether it is there now or not is their doing, so redo leaves it as it is.

    Redo, undo, and their order

  • Redo straight after undo gives back the graph from before the undo. Nothing has changed in between, so every row is taken back. The dump is the same, byte for byte, as the dump taken just before the un 655:
